title: It’s in the blood, Mr Bloom acceded at once. All are washed in the blood of the sun
html_source: There is a temptation to perhaps make more of these two sentences than Joyce intended. The immediate assumption is that Joyce is simply having Bloom state that Italian “impetuosity” is in the blood, and that “All are washed in the blood of the sun” is a pun on the Christian doctrine of redemption through the blood of the Son of God, or “blood of the Lamb” as the term is used in Lestrygonians. All three of the men are intensely emotional and romantic, in one form or another, Aquinas mostly in the chivalric sense. But it can be said that in each of the three flowed blood fired by religious conviction having been washed in the blood of the Son of God. Joyce often used Christian symbology and ritual as metaphor, and some argue that, regardless of his rejection of the Catholic Church per se, and his violation of Christian practice, in his more mature years, he realized that his faith was an inherent part of his identity, just as Bloom’s Jewishness was part of his, even while outwardly rejecting the tenets of Judaism. In this section in which the nature of souls, and their possible simplicity and the reconciliation between reason and belief is mentioned, it is highly unlikely that a reference to Aquinas is coincidental, despite the ironic word following “blood of the sun.”
